meta.title: AIS assessment readout - example deck (SYNTHETIC)
meta.audience: AIS leadership, with the service owners in the room
meta.fiction_notice: FICTION. Built only to exercise the deck-agreement engine against the example report. Not a University of Iowa readout and not a real assessment result.

slides.title: Why we are in this room
bullets: We assessed three service groups against four areas, using records you supplied.
This session presents three decision prompts for discussion.
Anything we could not evidence is shown as UNKNOWN rather than estimated.
speaker_notes: Open by naming the three decisions on the last slide so the room knows where this lands.
Say plainly that UNKNOWN means we did not have the record, not that the practice is absent.

slides.title: What this rests on
bullets: Seven supplied sources, each cited by exact version and locator.
Two sampled record exports, twelve records each, drawn from the assessed window.
Where one cycle of a record was supplied, we say so instead of generalising from it.

claims.text: IAM deployment records, twelve sampled.
IAM access review, one cycle only.

speaker_notes: If anyone challenges a number, go straight to S-A1 and read the locator aloud.
Prompt: is there a second access-review cycle we did not receive?

slides.title: What is already working
bullets: ESS change management: every sampled change carried a recorded test result.
That is the practice the two priority gaps should be measured against.
One further candidate strength is not corroborated yet and is held back.

claims.text: ESS recorded a test result on every sampled change.

speaker_notes: Name the ESS practice as the internal model - it is cheaper to copy a local practice than to import one.
If asked about IAM access review: one cycle was supplied, so it is a candidate, not a validated strength.

slides.title: The two gaps worth your time
bullets: IAM deployments: the procedure requires two approvals; most sampled records show one.
RIS recovery: backups complete, but no restoration exercise was recorded in the window.
Neither is a finding about individuals; both are about the record the process leaves.

claims.text: 58 percent of sampled IAM deployments record a single approval.
RIS backup jobs complete at 99 percent, which is not the same as a demonstrated restore.
Demonstrated recovery time is UNKNOWN - no restoration exercise was recorded.
Two ESS services have no recorded alert routing owner.

speaker_notes: Lead with the approval gap: it is the one with a cheap, checkable fix.
Do not let 99 percent backup completion stand in for recovery - say the difference out loud.
Prompt: were the five two-approval deployments different in kind, or just better recorded?

slides.title: Sequence, not a transformation
bullets: 0-90: enforce the approval record (R-001) and complete the alert routing table (R-003).
90-180: one documented restoration exercise per critical dataset (R-002).
180+: extend both practices to the remaining groups (R-004) once the first phases report.

claims.text: Approval record enforced in the first phase.
Alert routing owners recorded in the first phase.
Restoration exercise in the second phase.
Extension to the remaining groups last.

speaker_notes: Say what each phase produces as evidence; do not promise a maturity level.
R-004 deliberately waits on the first two phases reporting - that is the dependency, not padding.

slides.title: What it costs, and what we cannot cost yet
bullets: R-001: 80 staff-hours one-time, 4 staff-hours per month recurring.
R-003: 16 staff-hours one-time; review cadence not agreed, so recurring is UNKNOWN.
R-002 cannot be costed until dataset sizes and the restore target are supplied.

claims.text: R-001 one-time effort.
R-001 recurring effort.
R-003 one-time effort.
R-002 one-time effort is UNKNOWN pending dataset sizes and restore target.

speaker_notes: Give the two real numbers first, then the UNKNOWN, so the gap reads as scope and not as evasion.
Prompt: who can supply dataset sizes and the restore target, and by when?

slides.title: What we need from you today
bullets: D-001: enforce the two-approval rule in the IAM pipeline (0-90).
D-002: fund a restoration exercise for critical RIS datasets (90-180).
D-003: assign alert routing owners for the two unrecorded ESS services (0-90).

claims.text: Enforce, enforce with exceptions, or defer pending a wider sample.
Fund per dataset, pilot one, or defer pending the inventory.
Assign to service owners, to monitoring, or defer to the next review.

speaker_notes: Take the decisions in order and record the chosen option and its owner on the spot.
A defer is a legitimate outcome - record what evidence would change it.

bullets: EV-004 iam-deploy-export-2026H1.csv rows 2-13, version 2026-07-01.
EV-007 iam-access-review-2026Q1.pdf p.1-2, version 2026-04-03, single cycle.
These selected locators support the examples here; other findings retain their report references.

claims.text: Sampled IAM deployment records.
Single supplied access-review cycle.

speaker_notes: Read the locator, not the conclusion, when a number is challenged.

slides.title: Appendix - IAM approval sampling detail
bullets: Twelve sampled deployments; seven record one approval, five record two.
The procedure text requiring two approvals is IAM-DEP-PROC v2 section 5.1.
The sample is a sample - whether it is representative is an open input.

claims.text: Seven of twelve sampled deployments record one approval.
58 percent, rounded from seven of twelve.

speaker_notes: If challenged on representativeness, agree it is open and name the wider window as the test.

slides.title: Appendix - RIS backup versus restoration
bullets: Backup completion is read from the job log; restoration is a separate record that does not exist here.
No restoration exercise appears in the assessed window, so recovery time stays UNKNOWN.
This is an absent record, not an observed failure to recover.

claims.text: Backup jobs complete at 99 percent in the fictional log.
Recovery time is not assessed.

speaker_notes: Make the distinction explicit: a completed backup is an input to recovery, not evidence of it.

slides.title: Appendix - phase dependencies
bullets: R-004 depends on R-001 and R-002 having reported, which is why it sits at 180+.
R-001 and R-003 touch different systems and different owners, so they run in parallel in 0-90.
Each phase is described by the evidence it produces, not by a maturity level.

claims.text: Extension waits on the first two phases.
Approval enforcement in the first phase.

speaker_notes: If leadership wants R-004 pulled forward, name what evidence would be missing.

slides.title: Appendix - resource assumptions and open inputs
bullets: R-001 80 staff-hours covers the pipeline change and the backfill of approver records.
R-002 cannot be estimated without dataset sizes and the restore target.
Every UNKNOWN here is an input we asked for and did not receive.

claims.text: Pipeline change plus backfill.
Exercise cadence not agreed.
Complete and verify the routing table.

speaker_notes: Offer to convert any UNKNOWN into an estimate as soon as the named input arrives.

slides.title: Appendix - ESS change sampling detail
bullets: Twelve sampled ESS changes; twelve carry a recorded test result.
Procedure text is ESS-CM-PROC v4 section 3.2; records are ess-change-export-2026H1.csv.
This is the practice R-001 asks IAM to match for approvals.

claims.text: Twelve of twelve sampled ESS changes recorded a test result.

speaker_notes: Use this to answer 'can we actually do this here' - the answer is that one group already does.

slides.title: Appendix - ESS alert routing coverage
bullets: Nine ESS services in the routing table; seven name a routing owner, two do not.
The two unnamed services are the subject of decision D-003.
An unrecorded owner is a gap in the record, not proof that nobody responds.

claims.text: Two of nine ESS services have no recorded alert routing owner.

speaker_notes: If someone says 'we all know who responds', ask where that is written down.
